Economics is the study of how individuals, firms, governments and societies make choices when
resources are limited and human wants are numerous. The central problem is scarcity: land, labour,
capital, time, information and natural resources cannot satisfy every possible use at the same time.
Because resources are scarce, choosing one option usually means giving up another. Economics
therefore studies both the choices themselves and the incentives that shape those choices.
Microeconomics examines decisions made by individual consumers, firms and markets. It asks
questions such as why a household buys one product rather than another, how a firm decides its
output, and how prices coordinate buyers and sellers. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a
whole, including national income, inflation, unemployment, economic growth and stabilisation
policy. The two perspectives are connected: millions of individual decisions collectively influence
aggregate outcomes.

Scarcity means that resources have alternative uses and cannot satisfy all wants simultaneously. A
student who spends an evening preparing a presentation cannot use the same hours for another
activity. A government that allocates money to public transport has fewer funds available for
another programme. Scarcity does not mean that something is absolutely rare; it means that
obtaining more of one use requires a trade-off with another use.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. It is a
forward-looking concept: the relevant comparison is not every possible alternative, but the best
alternative that must be sacrificed. Opportunity cost helps explain why apparently free choices can
still be costly. For example, using an empty classroom for a meeting may have a low monetary cost
but a real opportunity cost if another valuable use of the room is displaced.

Positive economics describes statements that can, in principle, be tested using evidence. Examples
include claims about how a tax changes the quantity demanded or how unemployment changes
during a recession. Normative economics involves judgments about what ought to happen and
therefore depends partly on values. A statement that a government should raise taxes on a
particular group is normative because it contains a judgment about fairness or policy goals.
The distinction is useful because economic policy debates often combine facts and value
judgments. Evidence can help determine whether a proposed policy is likely to achieve its stated
objective, but evidence alone cannot decide how society should rank competing objectives. A policy
may increase efficiency while also changing the distribution of income. Economists can analyse the
trade-off, while the final normative choice may depend on social priorities.

A production possibility frontier (PPF) represents the maximum combinations of two goods or
services that an economy can produce with its available resources and technology, assuming
resources are used efficiently. Points on the frontier represent productive efficiency, points inside it
indicate underutilisation or inefficiency, and points outside it are unattainable with the current
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 3
resources and technology. The PPF makes scarcity and trade-offs visible in a simple model.
The slope of the PPF reflects the opportunity cost of producing more of one good in terms of the
other. If resources are specialised, the opportunity cost may rise as production shifts toward one
good, producing a bowed-out frontier. Economic growth can shift the frontier outward when
productive capacity increases through better technology, more resources or improvements in
human capital. A movement along the frontier represents a change in allocation, while a shift
represents a change in productive capacity.

section: 2.1 Demand and the Law of Demand
section_label: 2.1 Demand and the Law of Demand
text:
Demand refers to the quantities of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to
purchase at different prices during a given period, holding other relevant factors constant. The law
of demand states that, other things equal, quantity demanded generally falls when price rises and
rises when price falls. This creates a downward-sloping demand curve in the standard
price-quantity diagram.
A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve. A change in
another determinant of demand shifts the entire curve. Important determinants include income,
prices of related goods, tastes and preferences, expectations and the number of buyers. For a
normal good, higher income tends to increase demand, whereas for an inferior good, higher income
may reduce demand. Substitutes and complements also affect how consumers respond to changes
in related prices.

section: 2.2 Supply and the Law of Supply
section_label: 2.2 Supply and the Law of Supply
text:
Supply describes the quantities of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at
different prices during a given period. The law of supply states that, other things equal, quantity
supplied generally rises as price rises and falls as price falls. The usual explanation is that higher
prices can make additional production more profitable, encouraging firms to use more resources or
expand output.
As with demand, it is important to distinguish a movement along a supply curve from a shift of the
curve. A change in the product's own price changes quantity supplied and produces movement
along the curve. Changes in input prices, technology, taxes, subsidies, expectations, the number of
sellers and relevant natural conditions can shift supply. A fall in input costs, for example, can make
production profitable at lower prices and shift the supply curve outward.

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. The corresponding
price is the equilibrium price, and the traded quantity is the equilibrium quantity. If the market
price is above equilibrium, producers tend to offer more than consumers want to buy, creating a
surplus. Competitive pressure can push the price downward. If the price is below equilibrium,
quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage and upward pressure on price.
Equilibrium is not necessarily a statement that the outcome is fair or socially desirable. It is a
description of a point where the planned quantities of buyers and sellers are consistent.
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 4
Government intervention, market power, externalities and information problems can cause the
market outcome to differ from a socially preferred allocation. Nevertheless, the equilibrium
framework is a powerful starting point for analysing how shocks to demand or supply affect prices
and quantities.

Suppose consumer preferences change in favour of a product. At every possible price, consumers
now want to buy more, so the demand curve shifts to the right. If supply is unchanged, the new
equilibrium normally has a higher price and a higher quantity. Conversely, a fall in demand tends to
reduce both equilibrium price and quantity, assuming the supply curve remains unchanged.
Supply shocks work through the opposite side of the market. A rise in production costs shifts supply
leftward, generally increasing equilibrium price and reducing equilibrium quantity. An improvement
in technology can shift supply rightward, lowering the equilibrium price and increasing quantity
under standard conditions. When demand and supply both shift, the final result depends on the size
and direction of the two changes, so one variable may be predictable while the other remains
ambiguous without more information.

Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a percentage change
in price. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage
change in price. Because price and quantity demanded usually move in opposite directions, the
numerical elasticity is often negative; economists frequently discuss its absolute value when
classifying responsiveness.
Demand is elastic when quantity demanded responds proportionally more than price, inelastic
when it responds proportionally less, and unit elastic when the percentage changes are equal.
Elasticity depends on factors such as the availability of close substitutes, the share of income spent
on the good, the time available to adjust behaviour and whether the good is broadly or narrowly
defined. A narrowly defined product generally has more substitutes and therefore tends to have
more elastic demand.

Total revenue is the amount received by sellers from sales and can be written as price multiplied by
quantity sold. The relationship between price elasticity and total revenue is useful for
understanding pricing decisions. When demand is elastic, a price reduction can increase total
revenue because the percentage increase in quantity demanded is larger than the percentage
decrease in price. When demand is inelastic, a price increase can increase total revenue because
quantity falls proportionally less than price rises.
The relationship is a tendency within the relevant range of the demand curve, not a universal rule
that ignores context. A firm needs information about the responsiveness of its customers before
predicting the revenue effect of a price change. Revenue is also different from profit: a higher total
revenue does not necessarily mean higher profit because production, marketing and other costs
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 5
may also change.

Income elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a percentage
change in consumer income. A positive income elasticity is associated with normal goods, while a
negative value is associated with inferior goods. Cross-price elasticity measures how quantity
demanded of one good responds to a percentage change in the price of another good. Positive
cross elasticity is commonly associated with substitutes, while negative cross elasticity is
commonly associated with complements.
These measures help firms and policymakers understand relationships between products. For
example, if two products are close substitutes, an increase in the price of one may cause
consumers to shift toward the other. If two products are complements, a price increase in one can
reduce demand for the other. Elasticity therefore captures behavioural relationships that are not
visible from the price of one product alone.

Utility is a way of representing the satisfaction or benefit a consumer derives from consuming
goods and services. In the standard model, consumers face a budget constraint because income is
limited while goods have prices. The consumer's objective is to choose a feasible combination that
provides the highest attainable utility. This framework does not require utility to be measured in a
literal physical unit; it is primarily a model for ranking alternative consumption bundles.
A consumer's feasible choices can be represented by a budget line. A change in income shifts the
budget constraint outward or inward, while a change in one product's price changes the slope and
intercepts of the budget set. Consumer equilibrium occurs when the chosen bundle is the best
affordable option given preferences, prices and income. The model provides a foundation for
analysing substitution and income effects when prices change.

section: 4.2 Marginal Utility and Diminishing Marginal Utility
section_label: 4.2 Marginal Utility and Diminishing Marginal Utility
text:
Marginal utility is the additional utility obtained from consuming one more unit of a good, holding
other factors constant. The principle of diminishing marginal utility states that, beyond some point,
the additional satisfaction from successive units of the same good tends to fall. The first unit of a
good may satisfy an important want, while later units may satisfy progressively less urgent wants.
Diminishing marginal utility helps explain why a consumer may be willing to pay less for additional
units of the same product. In a simple model, consumers allocate expenditure toward goods by
comparing the additional benefit from spending another unit of money. The idea should not be
interpreted as saying that total utility necessarily falls as consumption increases. Total utility can
continue to rise while marginal utility becomes smaller.

section: 4.3 Indifference Curves and the Budget Constraint
section_label: 4.3 Indifference Curves and the Budget Constraint
text:
An indifference curve represents combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of
satisfaction. Curves farther from the origin generally represent higher utility in the standard
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 6
framework, and indifference curves are typically downward sloping because obtaining less of one
good requires more of the other to maintain the same satisfaction. Their shape reflects the
consumer's willingness to substitute between goods.
The budget line represents combinations that a consumer can afford. The consumer's optimal
choice is usually found at the highest attainable indifference curve, often where the indifference
curve is tangent to the budget line. At an interior optimum, the marginal rate of substitution is
related to the ratio of prices. A price change alters the budget constraint and can generate both a
substitution effect and an income effect.

Production uses resources commonly classified as land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Land
includes natural resources, labour refers to human effort, capital includes produced inputs such as
machinery and buildings, and entrepreneurship involves organising resources and bearing business
risk. Different industries combine these factors in different proportions, and technological change
can alter the importance and productivity of each factor.
Productivity refers to the amount of output generated from a given amount of input. Labour
productivity, for example, can rise through better skills, improved technology, more effective
management or additional capital. Productivity matters because it influences production costs,
wages that firms can sustainably pay and an economy's potential standard of living. However,
productivity should be analysed carefully because measured output can reflect many inputs
working together rather than the contribution of one factor alone.

The short run is a period in which at least one input is fixed, while the long run is a period in which
all inputs can be adjusted. The distinction is not a fixed number of months or years; it depends on
how quickly a firm can change its productive capacity. A factory may be unable to expand its
building immediately but may change its labour hours or raw material purchases more quickly.
In the short run, a firm may experience diminishing marginal product as more units of a variable
input are added to fixed inputs. In the long run, the firm can choose plant size, technology and
other inputs more freely. This distinction allows economists to analyse decisions about operating an
existing facility separately from decisions about expanding or redesigning productive capacity.

Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run, while variable costs change as output
changes. Total cost equals fixed cost plus variable cost. Average total cost is total cost per unit of
output, and marginal cost is the additional cost of producing one more unit. These measures help
firms decide whether to expand production and whether operating at a particular output level is
economically sensible.
Marginal cost often falls initially and then rises because of changes in productivity as variable
inputs are added to fixed inputs. The relationship between marginal cost and average cost is
important: when marginal cost is below average cost, average cost tends to fall; when marginal
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 7
cost is above average cost, average cost tends to rise. The minimum point of an average cost curve
occurs where marginal cost intersects it, under the standard smooth-curve model.

Perfect competition is an idealised market structure with many buyers and sellers, homogeneous
products, relatively easy entry and exit, and firms that take the market price as given. Because an
individual firm is small relative to the market, it has little ability to influence the price. The model is
useful as a benchmark for comparing industries with greater market power.
A competitive firm chooses output by comparing the additional revenue from another unit with the
additional cost of producing it. In the standard model, profit maximisation occurs where marginal
revenue equals marginal cost, provided production is worthwhile. In long-run competitive
equilibrium with free entry and exit, economic profit tends toward zero under the model's
assumptions, although firms can still earn a normal return for their resources.

A monopoly is a market structure in which a single firm supplies a product for which there are no
close substitutes within the relevant market, and significant barriers prevent competitors from
entering. Sources of monopoly power can include legal restrictions, control over an essential input,
large economies of scale or network effects. Unlike a perfectly competitive firm, a monopolist faces
the market demand curve and can influence price through its output decision.
A profit-maximising monopolist typically chooses an output where marginal revenue equals
marginal cost and then uses the demand curve to determine the corresponding price. Compared
with the competitive benchmark, monopoly can result in a higher price and lower quantity. The
analysis highlights a potential efficiency cost associated with market power, although real-world
monopoly policy must also consider innovation incentives, economies of scale and the costs of
regulation.

Monopolistic competition combines many sellers with differentiated products and relatively easy
entry. Firms may compete through price, quality, branding, design, location and advertising.
Because products are differentiated, each firm has some market power, but entry of competitors
limits long-run economic profit in the standard model. Examples often include restaurants, clothing
brands and other consumer markets where products are similar but not identical.
An oligopoly is a market dominated by a small number of significant firms. Each firm's decision can
affect rivals, so strategic interaction becomes central. Firms may compete aggressively, coordinate
implicitly, form explicit agreements where legal, or choose strategies based on expectations about
competitors' responses. Game theory provides a framework for analysing such situations by
examining players, available strategies, payoffs and the incentives created by each possible action.

Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the market value of final goods and services produced
within a country's borders during a specified period. The focus on final goods helps avoid double
counting intermediate inputs. GDP can be measured through expenditure, income or production
approaches, which should be consistent in principle because spending on output becomes income
to someone involved in producing it.
The expenditure approach commonly expresses GDP as consumption plus investment plus
government spending plus net exports. Real GDP adjusts for changes in prices so that changes in
measured output can be distinguished from changes in the price level. Nominal GDP uses current
prices. GDP is useful for tracking economic activity, but it is not a complete measure of welfare
because it does not fully capture distribution, unpaid work, environmental costs, leisure or many
aspects of quality of life.

The circular flow model illustrates how households and firms interact through markets for goods
and factors of production. Households supply labour and other factors and receive income. They
then use income to purchase goods and services from firms. Firms receive revenue from sales and
use it to pay workers and other resource owners. The model highlights the interdependence of
production, income and expenditure.
In an expanded model, governments, financial institutions and the foreign sector are included.
Taxes can be viewed as a leakage from the household-firm flow, while government spending is an
injection. Saving is a leakage and investment is an injection. Imports represent spending on foreign
production, while exports represent foreign spending on domestic production. The framework helps
explain why changes in one sector can affect activity elsewhere in the economy.

Economic growth refers to an increase in an economy's capacity to produce goods and services
over time. Growth in real GDP per person is often used as an indicator of changes in average
material output. Long-run growth can be driven by capital accumulation, improvements in
technology, better education and skills, stronger institutions, infrastructure and increases in
productive resources.
Growth is different from a temporary increase in output caused by recovery from a recession.
Sustainable long-run growth requires increases in productive capacity rather than simply using
existing resources more intensively for a short period. Growth can improve living standards, but its
benefits depend on distribution and on environmental and social effects. A complete assessment
therefore considers both the quantity and the quality of economic progress.

Money is an asset widely accepted for transactions. Its traditional functions are medium of
exchange, unit of account and store of value. As a medium of exchange, money reduces the need
for a double coincidence of wants in barter. As a unit of account, it provides a common way to
express prices and debts. As a store of value, it allows purchasing power to be transferred through
time, although inflation can reduce that purchasing power.
Modern economies use forms of money that are largely based on trust, legal arrangements and the
stability of the monetary system rather than on intrinsic value. Confidence is therefore important. If
people broadly expect money to remain acceptable and reasonably stable in value, it can
coordinate a large volume of economic transactions efficiently.

Commercial banks accept deposits and provide loans and other financial services. By connecting
savers and borrowers, banks can help channel funds toward consumption, investment and
productive activity. Bank lending also creates deposits within the banking system when new loans
are issued, subject to regulation, capital requirements, liquidity conditions and the demand for
credit.
Banks face risks including credit risk, liquidity risk and interest-rate risk. A bank must be able to
meet withdrawals and other obligations while earning sufficient returns on its assets. Regulation
and central-bank frameworks are designed partly to reduce systemic risk and maintain confidence.
The banking system therefore plays a major role in transmitting monetary conditions into
borrowing costs and spending decisions.

Monetary policy refers to actions by a central bank or monetary authority intended to influence
financial conditions and macroeconomic outcomes. A central bank may adjust policy interest rates,
conduct open-market operations or use other instruments to influence liquidity, borrowing costs
and expectations. The exact toolkit differs across monetary systems.
Lower interest rates can encourage borrowing and spending and may reduce the incentive to save,
increasing aggregate demand under standard conditions. Higher rates can restrain demand and
help reduce inflationary pressure. Monetary policy works with lags and is influenced by
expectations, exchange rates, credit conditions and the behaviour of households and firms. Central
banks therefore face uncertainty when choosing the strength and timing of policy changes.

Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time. A
common measure uses a price index to track the cost of a representative basket. Inflation reduces
the purchasing power of money when incomes do not rise at the same rate as prices. Moderate
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 10
inflation can occur in growing economies, but high or unstable inflation can complicate saving,
investment, contracts and household planning.
Inflation can arise from demand-side pressures, cost increases or changes in expectations.
Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's productive
capacity. Cost-push pressure can arise from higher wages, energy prices, imported inputs or supply
disruptions. In practice, inflation may have several causes at once, and identifying the dominant
mechanism is important for choosing an appropriate policy response.

Unemployment refers to people who are without work, available for work and actively seeking
employment, according to the definition used by a particular statistical system. The unemployment
rate compares unemployed people with the labour force. The labour force includes employed
people and those counted as unemployed, while people outside the labour force are not included in
the unemployment rate.
Unemployment can be classified by cause. Frictional unemployment occurs as workers move
between jobs. Structural unemployment arises when workers' skills or locations do not match
available jobs. Cyclical unemployment is associated with downturns in aggregate economic activity.
The categories can overlap, and the appropriate policy response depends on the underlying cause.
A strong economy can still have some unemployment because job matching takes time.

The relationship between inflation and unemployment is often discussed using the Phillips curve
framework. In the short run, stronger aggregate demand may reduce unemployment while
increasing inflationary pressure. However, the long-run relationship is not a simple permanent
trade-off. Expectations can adjust, and structural features of the labour market can influence both
inflation and unemployment.
Policy decisions therefore involve trade-offs and uncertainty rather than a mechanical choice
between two fixed outcomes. If policymakers attempt to maintain unemployment below a
sustainable level for too long, inflation expectations may rise. Conversely, aggressive disinflation
can reduce demand and increase unemployment temporarily. The challenge is to stabilise the
economy while recognising the lags and side effects of policy.

Fiscal policy refers to government decisions about spending, taxation and borrowing that influence
economic activity. During a downturn, a government may increase spending or reduce taxes to
support aggregate demand, subject to fiscal capacity and other constraints. During periods of
excessive demand, policymakers may reduce spending growth or increase taxes to moderate
demand. Automatic stabilisers, such as progressive taxes and unemployment-related transfers, can
change fiscal support without requiring a new discretionary decision each time.
Fiscal policy has distributional effects as well as macroeconomic effects. Different spending
programmes and taxes affect households and firms differently. The effectiveness of fiscal measures
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 11
also depends on timing, implementation capacity, household expectations and the monetary policy
response. Public borrowing can support demand during a downturn but creates future debt-service
obligations, so long-term sustainability matters.

The fiscal multiplier describes the change in aggregate output associated with a change in an
autonomous component of spending, under a specified model and set of assumptions. The basic
intuition is that one person's spending becomes another person's income, part of which may be
spent again. This can create a chain of additional expenditure.
The size of the multiplier depends on leakages such as saving, taxation and imports, as well as on
supply constraints and expectations. In a simple model, a larger marginal propensity to consume
implies a larger spending multiplier. In a real economy, the multiplier is not a fixed constant: it can
vary across countries, time periods and economic conditions.

Public debt is the accumulated stock of government borrowing that has not yet been repaid. Debt
can finance productive investment, smooth taxation over time or support the economy during
severe downturns. The key question is not simply whether debt exists, but whether the
government's fiscal position is sustainable given economic growth, interest costs, revenues and
future spending commitments.
A government can face increasing debt-service pressure if interest costs rise faster than its ability
to generate revenues or if persistent deficits continue without corresponding productive gains.
Debt sustainability analysis therefore considers the relationship among the interest rate, economic
growth rate, primary fiscal balance and the existing debt stock. The appropriate assessment
depends on the country's institutions, currency arrangements and access to financing.

Comparative advantage explains why mutually beneficial trade can occur even when one country is
more productive in producing every good. A country has comparative advantage in a product when
it can produce that product at a lower opportunity cost than another country. Specialisation
according to comparative advantage can allow trading partners to consume combinations that
would be difficult to achieve through self-sufficiency alone.
Comparative advantage is based on relative opportunity costs rather than absolute productivity.
Trade can create gains, but the distribution of those gains within a country may be uneven.
Workers and firms in import-competing industries can face adjustment costs even when consumers
benefit from lower prices and exporters gain access to larger markets. Trade policy therefore
involves both efficiency and distributional considerations.

The balance of payments records a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world over
a period. It includes current-account transactions such as trade in goods and services and income
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 12
flows, as well as financial and capital transactions. The accounts are linked because international
transactions involve corresponding entries reflecting how payments are financed.
A current-account deficit means that, in accounting terms, a country spends more on relevant
external transactions than it receives through the current account, with the difference financed by
other flows. A deficit is not automatically harmful: it may accompany productive investment and
future income. The sustainability and composition of external borrowing, exchange-rate conditions
and the economy's capacity to generate future income are important for interpretation.

An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in terms of another. Exchange rates
influence the domestic price of imports and the foreign-currency price of exports. When a currency
depreciates, exports can become more competitive for foreign buyers while imports become more
expensive in domestic currency, although the final effects depend on elasticities, contracts and
global conditions.
Exchange rates can be determined in markets through supply and demand for currencies, although
many countries intervene or manage their exchange rates to some degree. Interest-rate
differences, inflation expectations, trade flows, capital movements, political conditions and market
sentiment can influence exchange rates. A change in the exchange rate can therefore affect
inflation, trade, investment and the distribution of income across sectors.

Economic development is broader than economic growth. It includes improvements in living
standards, health, education, economic opportunities, institutions and the ability of people to
participate meaningfully in society. A country can experience GDP growth without equal
improvements in all dimensions of wellbeing. Development analysis therefore uses multiple
indicators rather than relying on a single measure of output.
Human capital is central to development because education, skills and health can raise productivity
and expand people's choices. Infrastructure, reliable institutions, access to finance and
technological capability can also support productive transformation. Development is often
constrained by interacting factors, so policies that improve one area may have limited impact if
complementary institutions or capabilities are missing.

Income inequality describes differences in income across individuals or households. Inequality can
be measured in several ways, including income shares and summary measures such as the Gini
coefficient. Inequality is distinct from poverty: poverty concerns whether people have resources
below a defined threshold, while inequality concerns how resources are distributed across the
population.
Economics Reference — structured for retrieval/chunking demos
Page 13
Some differences in income can reflect differences in skills, experience, hours worked,
entrepreneurship or returns to capital. Other differences can arise from unequal access to
education, discrimination, inherited wealth, market power or institutional structures. Policy
responses may include education, social protection, progressive taxation, labour-market
institutions and measures that expand access to productive opportunities.

Sustainable economic growth aims to increase wellbeing without undermining the environmental
and resource conditions required by future generations. Economic activity can create pollution,
greenhouse-gas emissions, congestion and resource depletion when private decisions do not
account for social costs. These are examples of externalities because part of the cost or benefit
falls on people who are not directly involved in the transaction.
Policy tools for environmental externalities include taxes on harmful activities, tradable permits,
regulation, public investment and support for cleaner technologies. The appropriate instrument
depends on the nature of the problem, monitoring capacity and administrative costs. Sustainable
development requires balancing current economic objectives with long-term environmental
resilience, while recognising that the costs and benefits of transition may be distributed unevenly.

• Concept query: What is the difference between a movement along a demand curve and a shift in

• Application query: What happens to equilibrium price and quantity when supply shifts left?
• Relationship query: How does price elasticity of demand affect total revenue?
